title: Waakye
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: The quickest of three documented versions — a tin of black-eyed peas, a cup of rice and baking soda standing in for the millet leaves that give waakye its colour.
longDesc: Waakye is rice and beans and it is the breakfast of Ghana, sold from huge pans with a tray of accompaniments beside it. The colour — reddish-brown rather than white — traditionally comes from dried millet or sorghum leaves, and the documented household versions substitute baking soda. This is the fastest of three: a 15.5-ounce tin of black-eyed peas, drained and lightly rinsed, one cup of white rice, half to one teaspoon of baking soda, half a teaspoon of salt, a tablespoon of oil, half a cup of chopped onion and two cups of water. Her note is that it cooks in about thirty minutes without burning.
ingredients: 15.5 oz tin black-eyed peas, drained and lightly rinsed — about 1 1/2 cups
equipment: Rice cooker, or a pot with a lid
steps: Drain and lightly rinse the tinned black-eyed peas.
Put the rice, peas, baking soda, salt, oil, onion and water into a rice cooker.
Cook until done — about 30 minutes, without burning.
Fluff and serve with the waakye tray: stew, shito, gari and boiled egg.
chefTips: Baking soda is the substitute for the traditional colouring agent. Waakye gets its reddish-brown colour from dried millet or sorghum leaves, and the soda approximates the alkaline effect.
Half to one teaspoon of soda is the printed range. More gives a deeper colour and, past a point, a soapy taste — start at half.
A rice cooker is what makes this the easy version, and her note is that it cooks in about thirty minutes without burning. Burning is the usual waakye problem.
Lightly rinse the tinned peas. The canning liquid is salty and would skew the seasoning.
Two cups of water to one cup of rice plus a tin of beans. The beans are already cooked, so the water is all for the rice.
Waakye is a tray, not a dish. It is properly eaten with stew, shito, gari, boiled egg, wele and sometimes spaghetti, all piled together.
Three documented versions use 2, 2.5 and 3 cups of water respectively for a cup of rice. This is the driest.
commonMistakes: Skipping the baking soda, which gives white rice and beans rather than waakye.
Too much soda, which tastes soapy.
Letting it catch on the base.
Serving it without the tray of accompaniments.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #27: Waakye 3 ways (rice and beans)', betumiblog.blogspot.com, 9 November 2009. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 11:03 PM'. NO YIELD LINE is printed. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Intro as printed: waakye is 'the classic rice and "beans" dish from Northern Ghana', with the pronunciation given as 'waatchy'. That is the basis for the northern attribution, even though it is eaten nationwide.

THE COLOURING AGENT: baking soda is noted on the page as standing in for kanwa or millet leaves. That note came from one fetch as a paraphrase rather than a quotation, so it is reported as the page's sense rather than its exact words.

VERSION 1, rice cooker, ingredients exactly as printed and confirmed on both fetches: 15.5 oz can black-eyed peas, drained and lightly rinsed; 1 cup white rice; 1/2 to 1 teaspoon baking soda; 1/2 teaspoon salt; 1 tablespoon vegetable oil; 1/2 cup chopped onion; 2 cups water. The '(about 1 and 1/2 cups)' note on the peas is SINGLE-PASS.
HER NOTE ON THIS VERSION, quoted, SINGLE-PASS: 'It cooks in about 30 minutes without burning.' The point being that burning is the hazard the rice cooker removes.

THREE VERSIONS ON ONE PAGE, published as three entries because their water ratios and bean treatments differ materially. Version 1 here uses TINNED peas and 2 cups water. Version 2 (GHA059) uses 1 cup DRIED peas, 1 teaspoon soda and 2½ cups water, with a brief boil and an hour's soak. Version 3 (GHA060 is a different dish; version 3 is recorded in GHA059's sources) uses coconut milk and cream. NOTHING IS AVERAGED.

A GAP, named: NO JOLLOF-VERSUS-WAAKYE COMPARISON was found in this post or anywhere else in the material consulted, despite both being national rice dishes. That is recorded as an absence rather than filled in.

ON THE WAAKYE TRAY: the full accompaniment set — waakye stew, shito, gari, boiled egg, wele (cow skin) and talia (spaghetti) — is how the dish is sold and eaten. No single source consulted publishes the whole tray as a recipe; its components appear separately at GHA051, GHA060 and GHA065.

THIS IS THE ONLY DOCUMENTED WAAKYE SOURCE in the material consulted that gives quantities for the rice-and-beans base itself. Zoe Adjonyoh publishes a 'Ghanaian rice' and a waakye lamb stew (GHA060) but those are the stew and a separate rice, not this base.
reheating: Steam, or microwave with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Rice and black-eyed peas together provide complementary amino acids, making a complete protein.
Black-eyed peas are high in folate, iron and soluble fibre.
Very low in fat as cooked.
culturalNote: Waakye is sold from dawn, wrapped in leaves or in a plastic bag, and the tray beside the pan is half the point — stew, shito, gari, egg, wele, spaghetti, assembled to order. It came south from northern Ghana and became the country's breakfast, and the reddish colour from millet leaves is the first thing a Ghanaian checks for.
